description_full: Intuitive Surgical, Inc. develops, manufactures, and markets products that enable physicians and healthcare providers to enhance the quality of and access to minimally invasive care in the United States and internationally. It offers the da Vinci Surgical System that enables surgical procedures using a minimally invasive approach; and Ion endoluminal system, which extends its commercial offerings beyond surgery into diagnostic endoluminal procedures enabling minimally invasive biopsies in the lung. The company also provides a suite of stapling, energy, and core instrumentation for its multi-port da Vinci surgical systems; progressive learning pathways to support the use of its technology; infrastructure of customer service and support specialists, a complement of services to its customers, including installation, repair, maintenance, 24/7 technical support, and proactive system health monitoring; and integrated digital capabilities providing connected offerings, streamlining performance for hospitals with program-enhancing insights. It sells its products through direct sales organizations, such as capital and clinical sales teams. Intuitive Surgical, Inc. was incorporated in 1995 and is headquartered in Sunnyvale, California.

financial_summary: Intuitive Surgical, Inc. is a large-cap healthcare business with a $138.3B market cap on $10.1B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +17% over the past three years and +15% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 21% against a 12% cost of capital — a 10-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 69% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $2.5B in free cash flow — roughly 25 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.06× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 40× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield is only 1.7%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 3.3× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 29% operating margin runs 30pp above the Healthcare median (0%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.

The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.05 across 465 companies in the universe; the top four hold 35% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 21% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has rebounded 9% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 34% below the high.

val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $108 (margin of safety -268%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 39%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $76.16 to $161 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Healthcare peers: P/E 48.3 vs 25.8, EV/EBITDA 30.7 vs 15.3 and P/FCF 55.5 vs 22.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 22% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 1.8% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The 30 covering analysts target $489 on average, 22% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 21% clears the cost of capital of 11.5% by 10pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.23).
It runs a 69% gross margin and converts 25% of revenue into free cash flow, or 17% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.06x.
ROE of 16% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.1x equity multiplier).
It spends 13.0% of revenue on R&D and 7.8% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $5.9B (4% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 34.9, in the safe zone).

growth: Revenue has compounded at 17.4% over 3 years, 18.2% over 5 years and 15.5% over 10 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 92% of profits supports about 19.3% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 16.9% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a backlog worth 39% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 14%.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (0.9x, 5.4% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 35, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.5%), and institutions hold 89%.
